title: The Matthew Effect of AI Programming Assistants: A Hidden Bias in Software Evolution
claim: A two-tier evaluation pipeline feeds algorithmic and framework tasks through multiple LLM assistants and coding paradigms to measure ecosystem-dependent success.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, dashed boxes group models and languages, feedback loops
description: A wide figure with two side-by-side flows. The left flow starts at a LeetCode logo. It passes through a crawler icon and a JSON file labeled Algorithmic Problems. The problems go to a dashed box of LLM logos (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemini-2.0-Flash, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-Turbo). They then go to a dashed grid of programming-language icons (C++, Python, Java, JS, Go, Rust, Erlang, Racket). Responses are saved to a folder and analyzed, and a long return arrow loops back to LeetCode. The right flow has two colored task boxes, orange for general CRUD applications and blue for divergent technology pathways. They merge through a Prompt arrow into a dashed box of tools (Cursor, Copilot, CodeBuddy). That feeds a vibe-coding arrow into an Agentic Coding box. The box holds a colored cycle of perceive, plan, implement, analyze, reflect and memory steps. An 'If fail' arrow loops back as iterative attempts.
caption: Two-tier experimental pipeline combining algorithmic tasks and framework tasks.
abstract: AI-assisted programming is rapidly reshaping software development, with large language models (LLMs) enabling new paradigms such as vibe coding and agentic coding. While prior works have focused on prompt design and code generation quality, the broader impact of LLM-driven development on the iterative dynamics of software engineering remains underexplored. In this paper, we conduct large-scale experiments on thousands of algorithmic programming tasks and hundreds of framework selection tasks to systematically investigate how AI-assisted programming interacts with the software ecosystem. Our analysis quantifies a substantial performance asymmetry: mainstream languages and frameworks achieve significantly higher success rates than niche ones. This disparity suggests a feedback loop consistent with the Matthew Effect, where data-rich ecosystems gain superior AI support. While not the sole driver of adoption, current models introduce a non-negligible productivity friction for niche technologies, representing a hidden bias in software evolution.
